dva-ini-073.text: Before applying an update to a stack of CloudFormation of production, the team wants to visualize exactly which resources will be created, modified or SUBSTITLED by the change — without executing it yet. CloudFormation provides this advance?
options: Change sets, which list the changes planned for revision before execution
Delete the stack and recreate it to see what changes
Stack Outputs
Drift detection, which applies the change and shows the result
dva-ini-073.explanation: The change set compares the new template to the current state and details each planned action (including destructive substitutions) — the previous revision that avoids surprises in production.
dva-ini-073.hint: The 'detailed budget for reform' before authorizing the work.
optionRationales: The change set compares the new template to the current state and details each planned action (including destructive substitutions) — the previous revision that avoids surprises in production.
Drift detection compares stack with template to detect manual changes — no update.
Destroying production to discover the effect of a change is exactly the disaster that the previous avoids.
Outputs expose created resource values — do not predict the effects of an update.

dva-ini-074.text: During creating a stack of CloudFormation, one of the resources failed to be provided. What is the standard behavior of the CloudFormation in this situation?
options: Run automatic rollback, undoing the resources already created to not leave the stack in half
Try to create the feature with default indefinitely
Transfer the stack to another region automatically
Keeps resources created and ignores the rest
dva-ini-074.explanation: By default, creation failure triggers rollback: the CloudFormation removes what it had provided, avoiding partial infrastructure and orphan — the state back to the previous one.
dva-ini-074.hint: Work that fails in the middle is undone: everything or nothing, by default.
optionRationales: By default, creation failure triggers rollback: the CloudFormation removes what it had provided, avoiding partial infrastructure and orphan — the state back to the previous one.
Maintaining half of the infrastructure is the behavior that the standard rollback avoids (there are options to preserve in troubleshooting, but it is not the standard).
No Infinite Loop — Failure Closes Operation and Turns Roll Back.
Stacks are regional and do not migrate alone — the reaction to failure is the local rollback.

dva-ini-076.text: No. Elastic Beanstalk, the team wants to implement a new version of the application without reducing the capacity available during the deployment, launching new instances in lots before removing the old ones.?
options: Rolling with additional batch, which adds an extra batch of new instances before replacing the old ones
Delete the environment and create another with the new version
All at once, which replaces all instances simultaneously
Simple rolling, which updates in batches reducing capacity during the process
dva-ini-076.explanation: This policy maintains the total capacity during deployment: the additional batch absorbs the load while the old batches are updated — at the temporary cost of the extra instances.
dva-ini-076.hint: Rolling 'with extra lot': first reinforcements arrive, then veterans leave.
optionRationales: This policy maintains the total capacity during deployment: the additional batch absorbs the load while the old batches are updated — at the temporary cost of the extra instances.
All at once is the fastest, but it knocks down the entire capacity during trading — guaranteed downtime.
Simple rolling takes out each batch of service while updating — capacity temporarily falls, which the requirement forbids.
Re-creating the environment generates total unavailability and loss of configurations — it is not a deployment policy.

dva-ini-077.text: In a service of the Amazon ECS configured with desired count = 4, what the ECS does when a task fails or is closed unexpectedly?
options: Migrate the cluster to another account
Automatically launch a new task to restore the desired count of 4 in progress
Reduce the desired count to 3 and follow normally
Pause the entire service until manual intervention

optionRationales: The service scheduler of the ECS keeps the desired state: monitors the tasks and replenishes those that fail, guaranteeing the quantity declared continuously — native self-recovery.
The desired count is the stated goal — the service does not lower it; it works to reach it again.
The replacement is automatic — pause everything for a task would contradict the orchestrator's purpose.
Clusters do not migrate from account — recovery happens in service itself.

dva-ini-079.text: An application will be implemented in dev, staging and production, and each environment uses a different bank and endpoints. What implementation practice avoids generating a different code package for each environment?
options: Use the same bench for all three environments
Edit the code manually on the server after each deployment
Build a single artifact and externalize the settings by environment (ambient variables), Parameter Store), injected in non-deployment
Compile a different package by environment with built-in values
dva-ini-079.explanation: 'Build once, deploy many': the same artifact tested follows for all environments, and what varies is the external configuration — eliminating the risk of divergence between packages.
dva-ini-079.hint: A single package travels on all stages; only the 'figurine' (config) changes on each stage.
optionRationales: 'Build once, deploy many': the same artifact tested follows for all environments, and what varies is the external configuration — eliminating the risk of divergence between packages.
Different packages mean that the staging test is NOT the binary that goes to production — classic release bug source.
Post-deployment manual changes destroy reproducibility and process audit.
Share bank between environments mix test data with production — serious operational risk.

Disable alarms during deployments

optionRationales: The CodeDeploy supports auto-rollback triggered by deployment failure or monitored alarms: if the alarm fires during deployment, the previous version is restored without human intervention.
